title: Short and long vowels
tip: Arabic has three short vowels, written as small marks (fatha, kasra, damma), and three long vowels written with the letters alif, yaa and waw. Hold a long vowel about twice as long as a short one: the length changes the meaning.
diagram: fatha (a) above the letter · kasra (i) below · damma (u) above, like a small waw · alif = long aa · yaa = long ee · waw = long oo
error: Saying every vowel the same length. kataba (he wrote) and kātaba (he wrote to someone) are different words.

title: ḥāʾ (ح) versus hāʾ (ه)
tip: For ح, tighten the throat as if you were breathing hard onto glasses to clean them: a strong, hoarse h with no voice. For ه, just breathe out as in English 'hat'.
diagram: ح: the middle of the throat squeezes, air is pushed through · ه: the throat is open, a light breath
error: Saying ح as a plain English h. ḥāl (condition) and hāl (halo) sound different.

title: Shadda: doubled consonants
tip: The small w-shaped mark ّ (shadda) doubles a consonant. Hold the consonant for a moment before releasing it, as in English 'book-case' or Italian 'pizza'.
diagram: a shadda sits above the letter; its vowel mark sits on top of it (or the kasra just under it)
error: Ignoring the shadda. darasa (he studied) and darrasa (he taught) are different verbs.

title: Emphatic consonants ص ض ط ظ
tip: Say s, d, t or th, but pull the back of your tongue up and back and make the mouth hollow. The vowels around an emphatic sound darker: a becomes closer to the 'u' in 'but'.
diagram: tongue tip in the same place as s / d / t / th; the back of the tongue is raised towards the soft palate
error: Saying ص as a plain s. sayf (sword) and ṣayf (summer) are different words.

title: ʿayn (ع) and ghayn (غ)
tip: For ع, squeeze the muscles of the middle of your throat while your voice is on, as if gagging gently. For غ, gargle softly at the back of the mouth, like a French r.
diagram: ع: middle of the throat narrows, voice on · غ: back of the tongue near the uvula, voice on, air rubs through
error: Leaving ع out completely. ʿĀʾila (family) needs the throat squeeze at the start.

title: Sun and moon letters
tip: The article al- (the) keeps its l before the 14 'moon' letters (al-qamar, the moon) but the l blends into the 14 'sun' letters, which are then doubled (ash-shams, the sun). The l is still written.
diagram: moon letter: الْقَمَر → al-qamar (sukun on the l) · sun letter: الشَّمْس → ash-shams (shadda on the sun letter)
error: Saying al-shams. The l is silent before a sun letter.

title: th sounds ث and ذ
tip: Put the tip of your tongue lightly between your teeth. ث is the unvoiced th of 'think'; ذ is the voiced th of 'this'.
diagram: tongue tip between the upper and lower teeth · ث voice off · ذ voice on
error: Saying ث as s or t. thalātha (three) is not salāsa.

title: qāf (ق) versus kāf (ك)
tip: ق is a k made much further back, where you gargle; the vowels after it sound deeper. ك is the English k.
diagram: ق: back of the tongue against the uvula · ك: back of the tongue against the soft palate
error: Saying ق as k. qalb (heart) and kalb (dog) are very different!

title: khāʾ (خ)
tip: Raise the back of your tongue towards the soft palate and push air through, like the ch in Scottish 'loch'.
diagram: back of the tongue close to the soft palate, voice off, air rubs through
error: Saying خ as k or h. khayr (good) needs the rough friction.

title: tāʾ marbūṭa (ة)
tip: Most feminine words end in ة. At the end of a phrase it is said as a short 'a'; when the word is followed by another word in a possessive phrase or gets an ending, the t is heard: sayyāra (a car) but sayyārat Sāmī (Sami's car).
diagram: ة looks like ه with two dots · said 'a' in pause, 'at' in a construct phrase
error: Saying the t at the end of a sentence: it is madrasa, not madrasat.

title: Long vowels ā, ī, ū
tip: A long vowel is written with a letter: alif for ā, yāʾ for ī and wāw for ū. Hold it about twice as long as a short vowel, as in English 'seat' against 'sit'. Many job words have one: طَالِب (ṭālib) and طَبِيب (ṭabīb).
diagram: fatha + alif = ā · kasra + yāʾ = ī · damma + wāw = ū · a short vowel is only a small mark
error: Shortening the long vowel (ṭalib instead of ṭālib), or stretching a short one: مُدَرِّس (mudarris) has no long vowel at all.

title: rāʾ (ر): the tapped r
tip: Arabic ر is a quick tap of the tongue tip just behind the upper teeth, like the r in Spanish 'pero' or the tt in American 'better'. A doubled ر (with shadda) is a short trill. Next to a and u it sounds heavy and dark, as in أَحْمَر; next to i it is lighter, as in كَرِيم.
diagram: the tongue tip flicks once against the ridge behind the upper front teeth; the tongue does not curl back
error: Using the English r, which curls the tongue back, or dropping it at the end of a word as in British English: أَحْمَر ends in a clear tapped r.

title: Tanwīn: the endings -un, -an, -in
tip: A doubled vowel mark at the end of a word adds an n: two dammas = -un, two fathas = -an, two kasras = -in. You hear it on words without الـ. The -an ending is usually written on an extra alif (شَايًا), but not after ة (قَهْوَةً). At the end of a sentence, careful readers drop -un and -in and say -an as a long -ā; set phrases such as شُكْرًا keep their -an in everyday speech.
diagram: two fathas above the last letter = -an · two dammas above = -un · two kasras below = -in · the n is pronounced but never written as a letter
error: Putting tanwīn on a word that already has الـ. A word has either 'the' or tanwīn, never both: خُبْزًا (bread) or الْخُبْزَ (the bread).

title: Hamza (ء): the glottal stop
tip: Hamza is the little catch in your throat in the middle of 'uh-oh'. It can stand alone (ء) or sit on a seat: أ, إ, ؤ or ئ. The seat is only spelling; the sound is always the same short stop. Say it clearly in the middle and at the end of a word: مَاء (water) ends with a tiny stop.
diagram: the vocal cords close completely for a moment and then open: a short silence before or after the vowel
error: Dropping hamza in the middle of a word. سُؤَال (question) needs a clear stop between the u and the a, and شَيْئًا (something) a stop before the a.

title: jīm (ج)
tip: In Modern Standard Arabic, ج is said like the j in 'jam'. You will also hear two local versions: in Cairo people say a hard g as in 'go' (gamīl for 'beautiful'), and in Lebanon and Syria a soft zh like the s in 'pleasure'. Understand them all, but use j when you speak MSA.
diagram: the front of the tongue presses against the hard palate just behind the ridge of the upper teeth, then releases with friction · voice on
error: Saying ج as y, or as a hard g in formal Arabic. masjid (mosque) needs a clear j before the d.

title: Hamzat al-waṣl: the vowel that disappears
tip: Some words begin with an alif that is only said at the very start of speech: the al- of 'the', and words like اِسْم (name) and اِذْهَبْ (go!). After a word that ends in a vowel, this first vowel drops and the two words run together: فِي الْمَدِينَة is fi l-madīna, and إِلَى الْيَمِين is ila l-yamīn. The alif is still written.
diagram: at the start of speech: al-yamīn · after a vowel: ila l-yamīn · the alif is written but skipped
error: Adding a catch in the throat or an extra a: fī al-madīna instead of fi l-madīna.

examples.en: what is your name? (to a man)

title: Word stress: find the heavy syllable
tip: Arabic stress follows a rule, counted from the end of the word. 1) A last syllable with a long vowel and a consonant (-ām, -īr, -āb) takes the stress: ḥam-MĀM, sa-RĪR, ki-TĀB. 2) Otherwise stress the second-to-last syllable if it is heavy, that is, if it has a long vowel or ends in a consonant: SHAQ-qa, MAṬ-bakh, GHUR-fa. 3) Otherwise go one syllable further back: NĀ-fi-dha.
diagram: light syllable = consonant + short vowel (ka) · heavy = long vowel (kā) or closed by a consonant (kat) · look at the last syllable, then the second-to-last, then the third-to-last
error: Putting the stress on the first or the last syllable every time, as in English or French. maṭ-BAKH and nā-fi-DHA sound foreign; say MAṬ-bakh and NĀ-fi-dha.

title: ḍād (ض): the letter of Arabic
tip: Arabic is often called لُغَةُ الضَّاد, 'the language of ḍād', because this sound is so rare in other languages. Say d, but press the front of the tongue firmly behind the top teeth and raise the back of the tongue, so the mouth feels hollow. The vowels next to it sound darker: ḍa sounds closer to the 'du' of 'dull'.
diagram: tongue tip behind the upper teeth, as for d · back of the tongue raised towards the soft palate · voice on
error: Saying ض as a plain d. darb (path) and ḍarb (hitting) are different words, and أَرْض (floor, ground) said with a light d sounds wrong.

title: Sukūn: a consonant with no vowel
tip: The small ring ْ (sukūn) means the consonant has no vowel after it: close the syllable on it and go straight on to the next consonant. ذَهَبْتُ is dha-hab-tu: the b stops, then the t follows at once. Don't slip a little extra vowel between the two consonants.
diagram: ْ sits above the letter like a small ring · consonant + sukūn closes the syllable: ذَهَبْتُ = dha · hab · tu
error: Adding a helping vowel: 'dhahabatu' instead of dhahabtu. Moving the vowel changes the person: ذَهَبْتُ (dhahabtu) is 'I went', but ذَهَبَتْ (dhahabat) is 'she went'.

title: Diphthongs: ay and aw
tip: When a fatha is followed by ي or و with sukūn, the two glide together in one syllable: ay as in English 'eye' (بَيْت bayt, house) and aw as in 'cow' (يَوْم yawm, day). Many Egyptians say bēt and yōm in everyday speech, but in Modern Standard Arabic keep the glide.
diagram: fatha + يْ = ay · fatha + وْ = aw · compare kasra + ي = long ī and damma + و = long ū
error: Reading بَيْت as 'beet' (a long ī) or يَوْم as 'yoom' (a long ū). The fatha before the letter tells you it is a glide.
